data.title: China shuts out Bloomberg reporter for shouting questions at Trump
data.description:
China blocked a Bloomberg reporter from being in the room to cover the opening remarks of President Trump’s trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

According to the White House press pool report, the Bloomberg reporter was blocked from the event because she asked a question during Trump’s bilateral with Xi earlier in the day. 

“A Bloomberg reporter was barred from this spray because she asked a question during the bilateral meeting with Xi,” the pool report read. “A WH official said they pushed to have her reinstated but Chinese officials insisted she be excluded.” 

Bloomberg reporter Annmarie Hordern had asked Trump during his bilateral with Xi if former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been disloyal to the U.S. Trump did not respond to the question. 

The move to shut out a journalist from covering a meeting is an example of China’s restrictions on press access. It is not unusual in the U.S. for reporters to shout questions at the president and foreign leaders during on-camera meetings and events. 

Trump appeared to criticize other press restrictions during the trip earlier on Thursday. 

“It’s too bad the media couldn’t see some of it, because every move was perfectly executed,” Trump said, referring to the summit. 

The three leaders addressed United Nations reform, oil production and supply, the International Criminal Court and nuclear conflict, according to text released by Russia and China.

data.title: Cassidy rejects Trump nominee to lead National Science Foundation
data.description:
A key Senate committee rejected the Trump administration’s pick to lead the National Science Foundation (NSF), just hours after the White House decided to pull the plug on its nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chairman of the Senate health committee, on Wednesday said Jim O’Neill, who previously served as acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and deputy secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services, would not be considered to lead the NSF.

If confirmed, O’Neill would have led the agency for six years. But Cassidy at the beginning of a meeting to vote on nominees said O’Neill didn’t have the support to advance and the vote had been cancelled.

O’Neill  “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements from [Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.],” Cassidy said.

“His role in the firing of Dr. Susan Monarez raised further concerns about the independent judgment he would bring to NSF,” Cassidy continued. “Several of the committee members had those concerns.”

Monarez was ousted as CDC director in 2005 just one month after she was confirmed, a move she attributed to her refusal to rubber-stamp vaccine recommendations from Kennedy that lacked evidence, or to fire employees without cause.

After Monarez was fired, O’Neill briefly became acting CDC director while continuing to serve as the number two official at HHS. He was then replaced as part of an agency-wide shakeup and nominated for the NSF post.

“I like Jim personally, but this time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right,” Cassidy said on Wednesday.

O’Neill does not have a science background. Prior to joining the administration, he worked extensively for venture capitalist Peter Thiel.

The NSF is an independent agency that funds basic research. It has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since April 2025, when Sethuraman Panchanathan, who was appointed during President Trump’s first term, resigned amid the Trump administration’s effort to cancel hundreds of millions of dollars of active grants and slash agency funding.

In April, Trump removed every member of the National Science Board, NSF’s presidentially appointed oversight body.

Cassidy, a physician, lost his primary earlier this year to a Trump-backed challenger.

 He has come under intense criticism from public health leaders for casting the deciding vote in committee and on the Senate floor to confirm Kennedy.

Cassidy on Wednesday said his committee would have endorsed Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration despite concerns about her role in the Trump administration’s vaccine policy, but the White House withdrew her nomination before the vote.

data.title: We're running out of time to fix America's fiscal crisis
data.description:
Now that the midterm elections are over, it is time for the Congress to get some important things accomplished in the lame duck session. Priority one should be to pass the appropriations bills for Fiscal 2027. It is essential that Congress avoid another costly and disruptive government shutdown. In addition, given the deterioration of the federal government’s financial condition, growing deficits, and rising interest rates and the related expense, it is time for Congress to take definitive steps to put our nation’s finances in order if we are to avoid a debt crisis. 

And it should begin serious thought about more fundamental change. We recently participated in a Harvard Law School conference on the Constitution’s alternative path for proposing amendments — the Article V convention. The conference involved both proponents and opponents of the need for amendments and how best to achieve them. It included discussion of potential fiscal responsibility, campaign finance, term limits, and other amendments as well as both methods for achieving such amendments. 

We agree that at least three constitutional amendments are needed — fiscal responsibility, campaign finance, and term limits. We also agree that if the Congress cannot or will not propose such amendments, the states must do so through the Article V amendments convention process.

Regardless of which method is used to propose amendments, we support using the individual state conventions of pledged delegates method for ratifying these amendments. This was the method used to repeal prohibition and is the closest thing to a referendum under the Constitution.

While reasonable people can and do differ on which topic should be pursued first and how best to achieve it, there was broad-based agreement that Congress has a clear conflict of interest with several of the most important subject matters. Specifically, restoring fiscal sanity and sustainability, term limits, and campaign finance. There was also broad-based recognition that the Congress has failed to implement an effective and transparent process to receive, store, and count state applications for a state-led Article V Amendments Convention.    

To address that conflict, Congress needs to pass legislation to delegate the related responsibility to the Comptroller General of the U.S., who is head of the Government Accountability Office. That agency is in the legislative branch, is professional, objective, nonpartisan, nonideological, transparent, and knows how to count. Congress previously delegated the related responsibilities for ratification of proposed amendments to the archivist.

Although there are several organizations pursuing efforts to achieve various amendments, there is inadequate coordination between these groups. This needs to change, given the difficulty in achieving constitutional amendments. 

Finally, Congress has demonstrated that it cannot deal with our large, known, and growing federal fiscal challenge through the regular order and on a piecemeal basis. Therefore, Congress needs to pass the bipartisan Fiscal Commission Act in the Lame Duck Session. Doing so would provide a much needed signal to the bond market that we are taking steps to change course and avoid the financial iceberg that lies ahead and threatens the fate of the USS United States. It is time for Congress to quit fiddling and do something before we hit the iceberg.

David M. Walker is former comptroller general of the United States and chair of the Federal Fiscal Sustainability Foundation. Lawrence Lessig is the Roy L. Furman Professor of Law and Leadership at Harvard Law School.

data.title: Trump, Xi, Putin issue 4-point 'declaration toward peace' after summit
data.description:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a four point “peace declaration” following their unprecedented summit in China on Thursday. 

The world leaders addressed United Nations reform, oil production and supply, the International Criminal Court and nuclear conflict, according to text released by Russia and China.

The declaration states that as permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, all three countries are “committed to promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges,” and intend to plan to “increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.” 

They also agreed “that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction,” and reaffirmed that a nuclear war must never be fought

“The three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons,” it reads.

Trump met Putin and Xi in Shenzhen, China, early Thursday for a historic 90-minute trilateral meeting, 

“We have a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful, and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people but the entire planet,” Trump said in opening remarks, before the meeting was closed to the press. 

“Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements, and we feel the opposite,” he continued. “I think that we are sure about that. No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about it. No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech.”  

The president indicated in the lead up to the summit that he would like to discuss the Iran conflict, the Russia-Ukraine War, as well as denuclearization. 

Washington has backed Ukraine in its effort to prevent Russia from taking over the country, while China has helped support Russia. Meanwhile, Iran has also received some aid from Moscow and Beijing in its war with the U.S.

On nuclear nonproliferation, China has resisted any checks on its buildup of nuclear weapons.

However, during Thursday’s bilateral meeting, Xi said, “nuclear weapons should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed, building a nuclear-free world,” according to China’s Xinhua news agency.

data.title: Rubio leads, Ossoff rises in 2028 polling
data.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio leads Vice President Vance in new polling on Republicans’ 2028 presidential field, while Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) climbs ahead of fellow Democrats. 

A new Emerson College national poll showed that, in an open-ended question about the race, 36 percent of Republican primary voters said they’d support Rubio for the nomination — a double-digit lead over the 20 percent that supported Vance. 

Another 7 percent each supported current President Trump, who is constitutionally barred from seeking a third term, and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), who challenged Trump in 2024. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who lost his House reelection bid to a Trump-backed primary challenger this year, also scored 7 percent. 

The scores mark a 30-point increase in Rubio’s presidential popularity since this time last year, and a 34-point drop for Vance. 

Trump has floated both top allies as potential presidential candidates. Vance, long seen as the heir-apparent, told Fox News this week that he would decide on running “sometime next year.” 

“My understanding with a presidential campaign is there’s a lot of infrastructure that you have to set up, fundraising, all that stuff and so, you know, you can’t declare a month before the Iowa caucus that you’re going to run for president,” Vance told the outlet. “So, you know, I haven’t made a decision. We’ll figure it out sometime next year.”

Rubio has said he’s not planning on a run next cycle, but that hasn’t quelled speculation about his future political ambitions. 

Across the aisle, Ossoff was leading other potential Democrats with 17 percent support from primary voters, but the field was still wide-open, with 32 percent of voters undecided about  who they’d pick for the next White House race. 

Ossoff, who just won another term in the Senate, committed along the campaign trail to serving out all six years and reiterated “zero interest” in a White House campaign, but political observers have continued to look to the Peach State senator as a rising star for the Democrats. 

Some have likened Ossoff to former President Obama, who famously said in 2006 that he would not run for the presidency as he served out his Senate term in Illinois, but later backtracked and ran in the 2008 cycle.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) came in behind Ossoff at 12 percent in the open-ended question about 2028, followed by California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) with 8 percent. Former Vice President Harris and former Biden-era Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg each brought in 6 percent. 

The scores are significant surges for Ossoff and Ocasio-Cortez, but a 16-point drop for Newsom and a 3-point decline for Buttigieg since November of last year. Harris was the clear frontrunner just after her 2024 White House run, but has dropped 31 points in the two years since.  

Ocasio-Cortez has played coy about her future plans. Harris has said she “might” run again after deciding against a bid to replace Newsom in California. Newsom, who is term-limited as governor of the Golden State, said this week that he’ll decide in early January whether to run for the White House. Buttigieg said in August that he was “more inclined than not” to run. 

The survey was conducted Nov. 14-16 among 1,000 voters. The credibility interval, similar to a poll’s margin of error, was plus or minus 3 percentage points.

data.title: Watch live: The Hill's Capitol Crypto Forum
data.description:
A new generation of financial infrastructure is taking shape through the development of blockchain networks and dollar-backed tokens known as stablecoins.

Central to this evolution is the Clarity Act — a comprehensive landmark bill that would create a U.S. regulatory framework for the cryptocurrency industry.

While the House voted to advance the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act over a year ago, it is stalled in the Senate. A tight legislative calendar, partisan ethics debates surrounding crypto business involvement by government officials and ongoing friction between traditional banks and the crypto sector over stablecoin rewards and DeFi regulation have all slowed momentum.

To explore what comes next, The Block and The Hill are joining forces to host the inaugural Capitol Crypto Forum on November 19th in Washington, D.C. For the first time following the midterms, lawmakers will gather with regulators and the blockchain industry to take a deep dive into what’s to come for digital assets.

Why is it important to bring digital-asset activity onshore, into a regulated US framework? What are the major hurdles preventing passage? How is passing the Clarity Act best for U.S. national security? What happens if it doesn’t pass? What are next steps for key regulators such as the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission? What happens next for crypto legislation in a new Congress?

Join us as we bridge the gap between Capitol Hill and the crypto ecosystem to map out the path forward for U.S. digital asset policy.

The event is scheduled to begin at 8:15 a.m. EST.

Watch the live video above.

data.title: With Kerch bridge strike, Zelensky shows he isn't asking Trump's permission any more
data.description:
Ukraine’s first major attack on the Kerch Strait Bridge was delivered by a truck bomb in October 2022, followed by strikes using unmanned surface vessels, S-200 rockets, and underwater explosives placed near pillars supporting the bridge.

This week, the Ukrainians finally finished the job.

As President Volodymyr Zelensky described it in a post on X, the operation surrounding the new strike had been “carried out over several weeks, developed and coordinated by the Security Service of Ukraine together with the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Our warriors gradually destroyed air defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective.”

Recall how, in February 2025, Trump lectured Zelensky in the Oval Office: “You’re not in a good position. You don’t have the cards right now.”

As of Tuesday, Zelensky had the cards. And he had given his own kinetic answer to President Trump and his envoys regarding their chosen path proposal on Tuesday: He would not let Trump’s meeting today with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin become Yalta 2.0, in which his country is divided up behind his back.

Last May when CNN’s Jim Sciutto interviewed Ukraine’s Ambassador to the U.S. Olha Stefanishyna’s, he asked her, “Is it safe to say Ukraine does have cards in this conflict?” 

Her response was priceless: “We printed them. … We made our own.”

That they did. According to Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara, “The [Kerch] strike was carried out exclusively with Ukrainian weapons — using our technologies and our solutions.”

Zelensky confirmed that domestically manufactured missiles and drones were used on both the road and rail sections of the bridge. That created an awkward backdrop for Trump’s meeting last night with Xi Jinping and Putin in Shenzhen.

The more Trump’s negotiation team has tried to advance its agenda, the more Zelensky has pushed back. And Zelensky has paid a price: His Starshield defense network service was throttled. His access to Patriot missiles was diminished. Yet he has fought the Russians to a standstill. And the Kerch Bridge attack may signal that the tide is turning in his favor. He is not about to abandon the Donbas region in exchange for promises of lucrative deals or economic opportunities.

For Ukraine and for Europe, national security takes precedence over both oil and mineral riches. As German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned during his visit to Kyiv in October, “If Russia is not stopped, it will turn its war machine against us sooner or later.”

The White House must adopt a different course of action. Instead of trying to make Ukraine quit, he should defund Russia. Waiving sanctions and seeking economic opportunities with Russia only keeps the Kremlin’s war machine going.

The White House must join Europe and enable Kyiv to defeat the Kremlin’s remaining source of power — aerial attacks.

Trump claims he wants to stop the killing. To date, Putin’s special military operation has yielded 1,629,010 Russian casualties — more than 54,000 in October alone. In the first 15 days of November, the Kremlin sustained on average 2,343 casualties per day — 35,145 casualties, nearly twice the number of Russian soldiers killed in its 10- year war with Afghanistan, and on pace for 70,000 by month’s end.

The best way to stop the killing is not to force Ukraine to give up — rather, it is to get Russia to stop attacking.

The Kremlin is displaying a false confidence of victory, with senior officials telling Putin-aligned lawmakers to “prepare for victory” in Ukraine. We have seen that before. In April 2022, as they drove the Russians back from their initial thrust toward Kyiv, Ukrainian forces found parade uniforms in their abandoned baggage. They thought they would be celebrating a victory within days of their invasion.

When Zelensky’s request for ammo fell short, he simply made his own and stopped asking permission. Persistence, resilience, adaptation and continued support from those still fully willing made Tuesday’s strike possible.

Needless to say, U.S. mediated trilateral negotiations are probably off the table in the near term. But there will be a Russian response, and the targets will likely be Ukrainian civilians in their homes. Kyiv will need to get its home-grown anti-ballistic missile defense system into the field sooner rather than later.

Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy They are the co-founders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

data.title: The Memo: Trump administration fails to quell concern over cascade of tech outages
data.description:
The Trump administration is not out of the woods yet on the knotty issues of cybersecurity, AI threats and creaky tech infrastructure — even though almost a week has gone by since the nation’s longest air traffic ground stop in a quarter-century.

The hours-long collapse of the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) air traffic control system last Friday was just the most dramatic moment amid a cascade of tech failures.

Outages, disruptions and malfunctions have hit other branches of government, such as the National Security Agency, and have affected some of the biggest brand names in American commerce, including Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase and United Airlines.

The White House and its allies have tried to tamp down the problems. President Trump himself declared, “It’s fine.”

“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen,” Trump told reporters near the start of his Asia trip.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking in the Philippines on Wednesday, told reporters there was “zero evidence” that the various incidents “are related to each other.”

Rubio also insisted there was no reason to believe the occurrences “have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyberhackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind.”

But even some usually loyal Republicans have seemed unpersuaded.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) told reporters at the Capitol on Tuesday that the full Senate ought to be briefed on the issue.

Referring to the official explanation for the air traffic control meltdown, Hawley said, “Maybe it’s because, you know, somebody unplugged a router in Arkansas or whatever. I dunno. I find that, frankly, a little hard to believe.”

More generally, Hawley admitted he was not sure what was going on.

“If this is all coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world. You can’t tell me that all of this just is happenstance,” he said.

To be sure, there are some challenges inherent to the situation that any administration would struggle to overcome.

For example, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has been candid about the fact that the precise cause of the air traffic outage has not been identified, even though it appears to have something to do with an upgrade and a router.

But there have been avoidable stumbles, too — including somewhat different messages from different members of the administration.

At a hastily convened White House press conference last Friday, just after the ground stop had lifted, Duffy appeared to dissent as Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin spoke about what caused the issue.

“What it appears to be right now is, as Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology, and that new equipment, new technology was overwhelming the older system,” Mullin said. Duffy, standing alongside him, looked down and shook his head.

Mullin also caused some consternation earlier this week when he cited an unnamed “one guy that’s very smart with tech” as the source of insight during an interview with Fox News.

This person, whom Mullin said was not Elon Musk, apparently contended that the root of the problem was the difficulty in making older software work in combination with the turbo-charged capabilities of artificial intelligence.

Beyond the specifics of Mullin’s performance, even some GOP-friendly voices express concern about the White House’s messaging.

At various times, Trump, Rubio, Duffy, Mullin and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton have all spoken publicly about the matter.

“They really need one person to be the communications lead and they need one clear message,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican strategist who is also the CEO of the Alliance for Secure AI. “As they get more facts, they can share those facts — and avoiding speculation as much as possible is a good thing. But we have got quite a few different messages.”

A consistent and reassuring message, Steinhauser added, was especially important on issues like cyberthreats and AI, which are evolving at warp speed and seem ominous to broad swathes of the public — even as the minutiae of how the technology works remains opaque to most people.

“The American people’s fears are rational,” he asserted. “We are entering a new era where things are going to get worse because AI is going to transform everything … Defensive capabilities are not going to keep up with offensive capabilities, so we are going to have a lot of instability in our critical infrastructure.”

The public’s nerves are frayed further because the spate of recent developments is taking place against a backdrop of the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and the broader challenge the U.S. faces from China.

Indeed, even as all the outages have been taking place, Nvidia — for a period the world’s most highly-valued company — has been roiled by the departure of its CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang amid allegations that a woman with whom he had an affair was a Chinese agent.

China denies this, and the woman, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen Huang — has not spoken publicly about the matter.

In terms of the outages themselves, a senior administration official told reporters on a Wednesday morning call that the precise causes were “disparate” but “in the upgrading and patching realm.”

But those statements don’t assuage the concerns — both technological and political — of those who fear that Trump’s tendency toward ebullient rhetoric is disconnected from public concerns.

“I don’t know what this president truly feels, but he certainly has not shown an appetite to talk about the dangers in a way that many voters would like to hear,” said GOP strategist Dan Judy.

“I think what most voters want is to be reassured that some adults in the room are keeping tabs on this — and I don’t think that’s what this administration is going for.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

data.title: Democrats worry Van Hollen's hard-line Iran stance could trigger shutdown
data.description:
Senate Democrats are pushing back on Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s (D-Md.) call to insist on adding language to any government funding bill to immediately end the Iran war, warning that stumbling into a government shutdown before the holidays would be a disastrous move.

Van Hollen’s demand to use government funding as leverage to shut down the 8 1/2-month military conflict with Iran is popular with the Democratic Party’s activist base, but Democratic colleagues in the Senate are pumping the brakes on taking a hard-line stance that could risk a shutdown.

The vast majority of Democratic senators, including Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.), whom Van Hollen is challenging, want to end the war immediately.

But they’re leery about overplaying their leverage ahead of the Dec. 11 government funding deadline.

After picking up nine Senate seats with Mary Peltola’s projected victory in Alaska and 43 House seats, Democrats on Capitol Hill want to avoid a potential shutdown they fear could derail their agenda ahead of taking control of both chambers in January.

“Nobody I’ve talked to thinks a shutdown makes any sense,” Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) said.

Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) warned “a shutdown of government right before the holidays is a tough nut.”

He called a shutdown a “dire situation” but said the Iran war has dragged on for months, and voters sent a clear message to Washington in this month’s election that they want the conflict resolved.

Hickenlooper declined to endorse Van Hollen’s call to insist on adding a rider to the funding stopgap that needs to pass by Dec. 11 that would block any appropriated funding from supporting the military conflict with Iran.  

Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) said Democrats “need to avoid a government shutdown” while finding a way to wind down the war as soon as possible.

“It is vital that we stay strong on bringing this war to a conclusion. It is vital that we fund the government and that’s the balance that we’re trying to find,” he said.

Van Hollen joined three Senate colleagues last week in a joint statement that called on Democratic leaders to insist that any short-term government funding deal includes “language that restricts the Trump administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”

Sens. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) joined the statement.

Senate Republicans are warning that stance will likely trigger another government shutdown — the third in just more than a year.

“I’m increasingly concerned that the Democrats may try to initiate another — a third — government shutdown this year and that would be a terrible outcome for the American people,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said.

“We do not need — we’ve already had two long, extended government shutdowns. We saw the impact that has on the American people. The American people don’t need another government shutdown. We need to make sure that people are getting paid,” he said.

Thune called Van Hollen’s demand to add language to any funding stopgap to prohibit any funding for the war “short-sighted.”

“They’re going to have the majorities, they’re going to have the gavels next year. I don’t know why you’d force another government shutdown,” he said. “That’s not a realistic ask. I understand he may be in the middle of a political campaign and feels compelled to do something like that, but it’s not good for the country.”  

A Senate Republican aide warned a shutdown could drag into 2027 and that Democrats might find it very hard to reopen federal departments or agencies once they take control of Congress next year.

The GOP aide also warned that triggering a shutdown could cause travel havoc ahead of Christmas, noting the 43-day government shutdown caused problems at airports after air traffic controllers began missing work after not getting paid for several weeks.

Van Hollen’s bid to oust Schumer from leadership and his call for Democrats to take an aggressive stance on defense funding, however, are winning plaudits from progressive advocates.

He received a standing ovation from a room full of progressive donors, union leaders and movement leaders at the Democracy Alliance conference in Washington on Wednesday, according to a person who was in the room.

Schumer, who is viewed as the favorite in the race to become Senate majority leader, said Congress should use its “power of the purse” to end the war. But he has spoken more generally about that goal.

“We’re going to end the war. … The Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” Schumer said at a press conference on the day after Election Day.

Senate Democrats discussed their strategy for the approaching Dec. 11 government funding deadline at a caucus lunch meeting on Tuesday.

Several Democrats called for finding a way to reach a funding compromise with Republicans to limit funding for the war without putting Congress at risk of stumbling into another shutdown.

“Everybody in our caucus believes that we should not be spending any more money to support the war and everybody in our caucus believes that we want to figure how to pass the CR. There ought to be a way for doing both of those things,” said a Democratic senator who requested anonymity to talk about internal discussions, referring to a continuing resolution to fund the government.

The Democratic senator said forcing a shutdown to end the war is a “ridiculous choice.”

“There’s no automatic reason that the only way to not fund the war is to have the government go into shutdown. That’s a ridiculous choice and that’s not the choice,” they added. “That’s what we’re talking about.

“Everybody is pretty realistic,” the lawmaker continued.

Van Hollen spoke up at Tuesday’s Democratic caucus meeting to defend his position. He argued that Democrats heard a clear call from voters to use their power to end the war now, according to a source familiar with the meeting. 

A second person familiar with the meeting, however, said Van Hollen did not go so far as to argue that Democrats should risk a government shutdown to cut off funding for the conflict.

data.title: House Republican pushes minerals, trade for peace in escalating Ethiopia, Eritrea crisis
data.description:
A House Republican is looking to leverage U.S. food exports, agricultural equipment and know-how to coax Ethiopia and Eritrea towards peace, in dual legislation expected to be introduced Thursday and shared exclusively with The Hill. The move also aims to draw the countries away from ties with China. 

Rep. Jim Baird (R-Ind.) is behind the Ethiopia SPARK Act and Eritrea PILLAR Act. Both texts call for the countries to take steps toward establishing a lasting peace and then benefit from formal trade talks to increase exports of American agricultural products, equipment and know-how.

“African nations are primed for partnership,” Baird, a member of the House Foreign Affairs subcommittee on Africa, said in a statement to The Hill.

“The continent is rich in natural resources and home to a young, growing population eager for greater economic opportunity. In Indiana and across America’s heartland, we have the agricultural expertise and technological know-how to help unlock that potential and build lasting economic partnerships.”

Baird’s legislation aims to trade progress on peace for Ethiopia and Eritrean access to foodstuffs like corn, soybeans, soybean meal and livestock feed, farm equipment, and agricultural research and technical expertise. It also aims to put the U.S. as a preferred partner compared to China, which has deep ties in both countries. 

“East Africa has tremendous potential, with the benefit of limited influence from America’s adversaries, like China,” Baird said. 

The legislation also calls for U.S. assistance in mining some of the region’s critical minerals: gold, silver, copper, zinc, iron, ore, potash, cement and limestone, natural gas and oil, among others, as well as access to the country’s port infrastructures. The U.S. could leverage reduced tariffs and better trade terms. 

“East Africa could seriously benefit from this economic opportunity, which can be a powerful foundation for lasting peace and prosperity,” Baird said in a statement. 

“Our engagement also sends a broader message across the continent: African nations willing to pursue peaceful cooperation and economic growth will find a willing partner across the Atlantic.”

Baird’s legislation comes as Ethiopia and Eritrea appear poised for all-out war, adding greater instability to a region already wracked with conflict. 

The Trump administration has also put forth diplomatic efforts. Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali on Oct. 14, discussing heightened tensions with Eritrea and called for a return to the 2018 Ethiopia-Eritrea peace framework. 

“The Secretary stressed that all countries in the Horn of Africa must respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors and avoid cross-border incursions. The Secretary emphasized that the region cannot tolerate more conflict.”

Troop buildups along the shared border have brought Ethiopian and Eritrean forces within striking distance of each other, Reuters reported on Wednesday. The buildup comes on top of an outbreak of fighting in September between the Ethiopian federal government and rebels in Tigray, which borders Eritrea. 

Democrats focused on Africa have also raised concern about the risk of escalating conflict, writing to Rubio in a letter dated Nov. 10 urging “sustained and coordinated diplomatic engagement” to lower the temperature. 

“The situation could lead to a multi-front conflict that would risk destabilizing Ethiopia the broader Horn of Africa, the Red Sea, our partners in the Gulf, and vital shipping lanes. The United States should bring new diplomatic energy and policy tools to bear before the conflict escalates further,” they wrote.
